title: Female dancer

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Fletcher Fund, 1928
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A small clay figure of a woman dancer, standing in a graceful pose in long clothing. Faint traces of paint remain on the pale, earthy surface.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, objectDate, medium, period (Tang dynasty, 618–907), creditLine, classification (Tomb Pottery), public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record (record has no tags)

context: This clay figure of a woman dancer was made in China during the Tang dynasty (618-907) and is classed as tomb pottery, meaning figures made to be placed in burials. Tang tombs sometimes contained figures of musicians and dancers. Traces of the original paint remain on the surface.

descriptions.k: This is a small clay dancer from long ago. She stands in a graceful pose. A little of her paint is left. How would you stand to copy her? Can you dance like her?
descriptions.g12: A potter in China made this dancer from clay more than a thousand years ago. She was painted, and a few traces of the paint are left. She stands in a graceful pose. Try to copy her pose with your body. What music do you think she is dancing to?
descriptions.g35: This dancer comes from Tang dynasty China, made of earthenware and once painted. Only traces of color remain. Tang tombs often held figures of dancers and musicians, so the dead could have entertainment. Look at her pose and her clothing. How does the potter make a still figure seem to move? What do you think the music might sound like?
descriptions.g68: This Tang earthenware figure of a dancer retains only traces of its original pigment, so we must imagine how bright it once looked. Tomb pottery of this kind often included entertainers such as dancers and musicians, reflecting a taste for music and performance at the Tang court and in elite life. How does the pose suggest movement or rhythm? What details of clothing and posture matter most, and how might paint have changed the effect?
descriptions.g910: A Tang tomb figure of a dancer, this earthenware sculpture invites questions about performance, loss, and imagination. Only traces of pigment survive, so what we see is partly the effect of time. The pose, balancing stillness and implied movement, conveys the grace associated with Tang performance, though the Met's record does not specify a dance or occasion. Consider how the potter uses posture, drapery, and proportion to suggest rhythm, and how burial context shapes what such figures mean.
descriptions.g1112: This 7th-8th century dancer was made for burial, which raises questions about why entertainers appear in tombs: as sources of pleasure for the afterlife, as signs of status, or as reflections of living culture. The record's note of traces of pigment reminds us that our view of it is partial, as paint has largely worn away. A figure that stills a moving art form also asks how sculpture can capture time. Which readings can the evidence support, and which remain speculative?

teacherNote.context: A Tang dynasty (7th-8th century) tomb figure of a dancer, earthenware with traces of pigment. Confirm clothing and pose details from the image before class discussion.
directions: Have students strike the dancer's pose and describe which muscles and balance it needs.
Ask students to imagine and sketch the dancer in full color, then compare their ideas.
Discuss how artists show movement in still works and find examples in the archive.
